words.lemma: brá (slab); read as brá 'brow' used of a shore, or a scribal/OCR variant of brú 'brink, edge' (dat. sg. after ar)

words.etymon: lókus (Gk λάκκος ~ Lat. lacus, OIr. loch)

cognate: Two cognate nouns in the same relation: *h₃bʰruH- 'brow' (Ir. brá/brú, Gk ὀφρύς) as the high edge or rim of a body of water, with *lókus- (Ir. loch, Gk λάκκος) as the water it borders.
drift_or_renewal: Gk λάκκος has narrowed to 'pit, pond, cistern' (here a salt pond the size of a lake, next to λίμνη); Ir. loch keeps 'lake'. In the usual Irish phrase the brow word is brú/bruach 'brink', and its link to brá 'eyebrow' and to *h₃bʰruH- is not certain (some put brú 'brink' with brú 'belly'). The Irish anchor uses brá, the 'eyebrow' word itself.
shared_syntax: Irish: preposition (for/ar) + brow-noun + genitive of the water (for brú in locha / mara). Greek: ἐπί + ὀφρύς + genitive of the shore, river or place (ἐπ’ ὀφρύσι Πακτωλοῖο, ἐπ’ ὀφρύος αἰγιαλοῖο; Homer ἐπ’ ὀφρύσι Καλλικολώνης of a hill). In the Strabo anchor it is instead a pond enclosed by high ὀφρύες. The prepositions are not cognate (for < *uper; ἐπί).
context: Both anchors are topographic descriptions of a lake edge: the Irish saint's life (Beatha Lasrach, MS 1670; this line comes from the edition's variant/notes and is OCR) has the saints blessing 'on the brow of the green lake', and Strabo describes a salt pond ringed by steep high brows. The Irish phrase is old and fixed: it runs from Old Irish (for brú ind locha, for bru in mara) through the annals into Early Modern Irish (ar bruach an locha). The Greek phrase is Homeric for a hill and Hellenistic-poetic for shores and rivers.
phrase: 'on the brow of the lake/shore' — Ir. for/ar brú (brá) in locha ~ Gk ἐπ’ ὀφρύσι + gen. of water; Strabo λάκκος … ὀφρύσι

note: All 160 bundles read; all pivots are Early Modern Irish (medical, astronomical, hagiographic, romance prose, mostly OCR) against mostly Greek prose partners. Only one weak lead. Dropped: BC-053ad (Ir. ni ber troigh techid ~ Serb. da od vraga ne uteče traga: cognate verb *tekʷ- 'flee', but 'foot'~'trace' is unverified and the syntax differs; Serbian ne uteče X is a generic annihilation formula). BC-0d04b (clú fan cruinne): no cognate partner.
